label: Gaussian and Chi-square Distributions
notes: This short appendix on printed pages 565 to 567 supplies the statistical bridge of multiple-view geometry. A vision residual is not just a length; it is a vector measured in the units and correlations of its covariance. We turn residual magnitudes into calibrated acceptance tests using Gaussian models, Mahalanobis distance, and chi-square gates.

label: The Multivariate Gaussian
notes: The multivariate Gaussian is fixed by a mean vector and a covariance matrix. Its negative log density is, up to a constant, half the squared Mahalanobis distance, so the level sets of the density are exactly the ellipsoids of constant covariance-weighted distance. Diagonal entries set marginal variance; off-diagonal entries encode correlation.

label: Covariance Sets the Ellipse
notes: Reading the covariance geometrically is the key skill here. Eigenvectors give the principal axes of the uncertainty ellipse and eigenvalues give the squared semi-axis lengths. Correlation rotates the ellipse away from the coordinate axes. A one-pixel residual along a noisy direction must not count the same as one along a tightly constrained direction.

label: Mahalanobis Distance
notes: Mahalanobis distance is the central object. The squared form is the residual sandwiched around the inverse covariance, which is exactly ordinary squared length measured after whitening. Whitening multiplies residuals by the inverse square root of covariance, turning an anisotropic correlated cloud into an isotropic unit cloud where Euclidean comparison is finally fair.

label: Whitening the Residual Cloud
notes: This slide shows whitening as a coordinate change. The raw correlated ellipse maps to a circle once we apply the inverse square root of the covariance. In whitened coordinates the covariance becomes the identity, every direction carries equal uncertainty, and a Mahalanobis gate becomes a plain circular radius test.

label: Mahalanobis Follows Chi-square
notes: Here is the distributional fact that makes gates calibrated. If a residual of rank r is truly zero-mean Gaussian with the assumed covariance, its squared Mahalanobis distance follows a chi-square distribution with r degrees of freedom. Equivalently, chi-square is a sum of r independent squared standardized residuals, one per whitened coordinate.

label: Chi-square Confidence Gates
notes: A confidence gate accepts a residual when its squared Mahalanobis distance falls below a chi-square quantile at the chosen probability. We read off the 68, 95, and 99 percent thresholds for two degrees of freedom. These thresholds are ellipses in residual coordinates and concentric circles in whitened coordinates, the same gate seen two ways.

label: The Chi-square Density
notes: The chi-square density shifts right and flattens as degrees of freedom grow, so the same probability level demands a larger threshold for larger residual vectors. The shaded tail beyond the quantile is the false-rejection rate. Forgetting that the threshold depends on residual rank is a classic calibration error in reconstruction pipelines.

label: Residual Diagnostics
notes: The gate is only as good as the covariance model. If residuals are correctly modeled, their squared Mahalanobis values histogram onto the chi-square density and empirical gate coverage matches the target probabilities. Mismatch flags underestimated covariance, ignored correlation, or outliers. This diagnostic is a cheap, decisive health check for an estimator.

label: RANSAC and Goodness of Fit
notes: Chi-square gating drives two everyday tasks. In RANSAC the inlier threshold is a chi-square quantile on per-point reprojection or Sampson residuals, not an arbitrary pixel number. As a goodness-of-fit test, the total summed squared residual is compared against chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of constraints minus parameters.

label: Pitfalls and Takeaways
notes: Close on the failure modes. Euclidean gates on anisotropic residuals reject good points and accept bad ones. The degrees of freedom must track residual rank. A non-positive-definite or badly scaled covariance makes distance meaningless, and a singular covariance forces the pseudo-inverse with rank in place of dimension. Density near the mean is not acceptance.
